hmmt-feb-2002-geo-05.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2002-geo-05.body:
Take square $ABCD$ with midpoints $E,F,G,H$ of $AB,BC,CD,DA$, and lines $AF,BG,CH,DE$ (each corner and each midpoint used once). They bound a small square $IJKL$ in the middle ($I=AF\cap DE$, $J=BG\cap AF$, $K=CH\cap BG$, $L=DE\cap CH$).

Coordinates: $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(1,1)$, $D=(0,1)$, $F=(1,\frac12)$, $G=(\frac12,1)$, $E=(\frac12,0)$, $H=(0,\frac12)$. Line $AF$: $y=\frac x2$. Line $BG$: $y=-2(x-1)$. They meet at $J$: $\frac x2=2-2x\Rightarrow x=\frac45$, $y=\frac25$. Line $DE$: $y=1-2x$; it meets $AF$ at $\frac x2=1-2x\Rightarrow x=\frac25$, $y=\frac15$, which is $I$. Then $IJ=\sqrt{\left(\frac25\right)^2+\left(\frac15\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt5}5$, so the area of the square is $\frac15$.

**Answer: 1/5**

hmmt-feb-2002-geo-06.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2002-geo-06.body:
The lower-left corner $(u,v)$ of the unit square is uniform on $0\le u\le4$, $0\le v\le4$ (area $16$). The point $(4.5,0.5)$ lies in the square iff $u\le4.5\le u+1$ and $v\le0.5\le v+1$, i.e. $3.5\le u\le4$ and $0\le v\le0.5$, a region of area $\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14$. The probability is $\frac{1/4}{16}=\frac1{64}$.

**Answer: 1/64**

hmmt-feb-2002-geo-07.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2002-geo-07.body:
The minimal triangle is the equilateral triangle whose sides lie along the lines $DG$, $EH$, $FI$ (the lines through the two corners of adjacent squares at each vertex of $ABC$); the other natural candidate, with sides along $DE$, $FG$, $HI$, is larger.

Let $O$ be the centre of $ABC$, so $OB=\frac2{\sqrt3}$. At vertex $B$, $BD=BG=2$ and $\angle DBG=360^\circ-90^\circ-90^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$, so line $DG$ is perpendicular to the ray $OB$ at distance $2\cos60^\circ=1$ beyond $B$. Hence the distance from $O$ to each side of the big triangle is $r=\frac2{\sqrt3}+1$, and its side length is $2\sqrt3\,r=4+2\sqrt3$. The area is $\frac{\sqrt3}4(4+2\sqrt3)^2=\frac{\sqrt3}4(28+16\sqrt3)=12+7\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $12+7\sqrt3$**

hmmt-feb-2002-geo-08.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2002-geo-08.body:
Each square lies on the same side of its base as the triangle, so the squares overlap the triangle. The minimal containing triangle is the (inverted) equilateral triangle with sides along the far sides $DE$, $FG$, $HI$ of the squares.

Let $O$ be the centre of $ABC$; the distance from $O$ to $AB$ is $\frac1{\sqrt3}$, and side $DE$ is at distance $2$ from $AB$ on the triangle's side, i.e. at distance $2-\frac1{\sqrt3}$ from $O$ on the other side. So the big triangle has inradius $2-\frac1{\sqrt3}$ and side $2\sqrt3\left(2-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)=4\sqrt3-2$. Its area is $\frac{\sqrt3}4(4\sqrt3-2)^2=\frac{\sqrt3}4(52-16\sqrt3)=13\sqrt3-12$.

**Answer: $13\sqrt3-12$**

hmmt-feb-2002-geo-10.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2002-geo-10.body:
The side length is $AC=12$. Place $A=(0,0)$, $B=(12,0)$, $C=(6,6\sqrt3)$. Then $E=(3,3\sqrt3)$, $F=(9,0)$, and $D=C+\frac4{12}(B-C)=(8,4\sqrt3)$. So $\vec{EF}=(6,-3\sqrt3)$ and $\vec{ED}=(5,\sqrt3)$. Then $\vec{EF}\cdot\vec{ED}=30-9=21$, $|EF|=\sqrt{63}$, $|ED|=\sqrt{28}$, so $\cos\angle DEF=\frac{21}{\sqrt{63\cdot28}}=\frac{21}{42}=\frac12$ and $\angle DEF=60^\circ$.

**Answer: 60**
